title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
pattern: DFS carrying the maximum seen on the path
statement: A node of a binary tree is **good** if no node on the path from the root down to it has a larger value. Return the number of good nodes.

example.why: Good nodes: the root 3, the node 4, the node 5, and the lower 3 (path 3 → 1 → 3 has nothing above 3).

idea: Whether a node is good depends only on the **largest value above it** on its own path from the root.
So walk down with DFS and pass that maximum along as an argument.
A node is good if its value is at least that maximum; in that case it also becomes the new maximum for everything below it.

complexity.spaceWhy: The recursion stack is as deep as the tree's height h.

steps.text: Our example: **`root = [3,1,4,3,None,1,5]`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
The root has nothing above it, so it is always **good**.
Node 1: a bigger value, 3, sits above it on this path. **Not good**.
Node 3: the largest value above it on this path is 3. Nothing above is bigger than 3, so it is **good**.
An empty spot contains no good nodes: return 0.
The subtree of node 1 contains **1 good node**. (The small labels are these counts.)
Node 4: the largest value above it on this path is 3. Nothing above is bigger than 4, so it is **good**.
Node 1: a bigger value, 4, sits above it on this path. **Not good**.
Node 5: the largest value above it on this path is 4. Nothing above is bigger than 5, so it is **good**.
The subtree of node 4 contains **2 good nodes**. (The small labels are these counts.)
The subtree of node 3 contains **4 good nodes**. (The small labels are these counts.)
Done — the answer is **`4`**. Good nodes: the root 3, the node 4, the node 5, and the lower 3 (path 3 → 1 → 3 has nothing above 3).
